newsitem.title: THAILAND: INTERVIEW-Erratic weather to change Thai farming.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Erratic weather to change Thai farming.

text.p: Erratic weather patterns in Thailand will force farmers to change crop planting schedules and habits, a senior agriculture ministry official said on Thursday.
Ananta Dalodom, deputy permanent secretary of agriculture, told Reuters a longer dry season had been detected in recent years.
The government was campaigning to persuade farmers to change their planting habits so as to maximise their gains, he said.
"For example, we have advised farmers to start planting rice in August instead of July. Not only for this year but also for the future," Ananta said.
Thailand's rainy season normally starts in April or May, followed by a brief dry period in June. It then resumes in July or August.
But in recent years, the dry spell during the rainbreak has become more severe, Ananta said.
"The problem has become a pattern in the past several years. It might be caused by rising temperatures at the centre of the earth, the greenhouse effect and changes in the environment," he said.
But the effort to change traditional practices has not been much of a success so far.
"Old habits die hard. Farmers have been using the old crop season for decades," Ananta said.
Good crop prices, especially for rice, and credit supports for corn have also lured farmers into sowing at the first sight of rain.
Farmers normally start planting their first corn crop in April and the crop usually enters the tasseling period by June.
But a long dry spell during that crucial stage this year wreaked havoc on the first corn crop. More than 352,000 hectares of corn planting area was damaged, Ananta said.
He suggested that corn be planted around August to ensure sufficient water.
"The problem is we grow corn too early and risk the damage caused by insufficient rain and then harvest it during the rainy season," he said.

"This practice causes problems with the quality of the corn because of high moisture content which could lead to alpha toxins. Why don't we grow corn in August and harvest in November which is the start of winter?"
But with the change in planting habits, Ananta said the challenge lay in the farm sector's ability to improve productivity to offset the weather.
"The agriculture ministry has been consistently developing new agriculture technology, including developing new strains to improve output in view of these changes," he said.
However, Ananta said it was too soon to say if there would be a drought this year or if the long dry spell was caused by the effects of the El Nino weather phenomenon.
The El Nino effect, a warm current of water in the Pacific, can upset global weather patterns for up to 18 months, depending on how soon ocean temperatures return to normal.
"It would be too early to draw a conclusion. The Thai Meteorological Department has forecast that there will be ample rainfall later this year," Ananta said.
